title: Impact of high-power short-duration atrial fibrillation ablation technique on the incidence of silent cerebral embolism: a prospective randomized controlled study
one_line: A 100-patient 1:1 randomized trial testing whether high-power short-duration (50 W) AF ablation with the 56-hole Smart Touch Surround Flow catheter reduces silent cerebral embolism versus conventional 30-35 W Smart Touch ablation, assessed by 1 mm high-resolution diffusion-weighted MRI.
key_claims: New silent cerebral embolism occurred in 22/50 (44%) of HPSD patients versus 20/50 (40%) of conventional patients (p = 0.685), with no difference in average lesion number (p = 0.751), maximum lesion diameter (p = 0.405), or total lesion volume per patient (p = 0.669).

Post-procedural hDWI detected 106 new lesions across 42/100 patients (42%); per the episode, 92% were in the telencephalon and 8% in the cerebellum, with 50% <3 mm, 49% 3-10 mm and only one lesion >10 mm.
Multivariable regression identified persistent AF and CHA2DS2-VASc score as the independent determinants of SCE, while catheter type and ablation duration were not predictive.
MoCA scores did not differ between patients with and without SCE immediately post-procedure (p = 0.572) or at 3-month follow-up (p = 0.743).
The HPSD/STSF arm was procedurally faster and used less irrigation fluid, confirming the technique delivered its intended efficiency benefit (episode framing of the paper's procedural data).
limitations: Authors explicitly note the small sample size of 100 patients, which may be underpowered to detect modest between-group differences.
Median patient age 63, 60% male, 59% paroxysmal AF — a single-cohort population enrolled June 2020-September 2021, limiting generalisability.
Additional ablation lesions beyond pulmonary vein isolation were left to operator discretion, introducing procedural heterogeneity.
Imaging follow-up was only 24-72 h post-ablation; lesion resolution and later imaging were not assessed in this trial.
Cognitive follow-up stopped at 3 months, so long-term or cumulative cognitive effects of repeated micro-embolism were not tested.

The mechanistic account of stagnant left-atrial flow overwhelming catheter cooling, and of microglial/collateral-circulation lesion clearance within 2-4 weeks, was narrative interpretation rather than measured in this study.
open_questions: Would a larger, adequately powered trial detect a real but modest SCE reduction from HPSD/STSF that this 100-patient study could not?
Does serial MRI confirm that these sub-10 mm lesions resolve rather than persist, and do repeated ablations accumulate damage?
Would longer cognitive follow-up beyond 3 months, with tests more sensitive than MoCA, reveal subtle decline in SCE-positive patients?
Can pre-procedural modification of left-atrial blood flow or anticoagulation strategy reduce SCE more effectively than catheter design?
